British Museum’s £33 tickets sold out in a day but some slots have been reserved for guests at five-star One Aldwych Those hoping to snare a glimpse of the Bayeux tapestry when it comes to the British Museum this September faced nine-hour online queues, with the £33 tickets sold out within a day. But the monied guests of a five-star hotel in Covent Garden have not had to go to such arduous lengths to get a view of the nearly 1,000-year-old depiction of William the Conqueror’s victory over King Harold II of England at Hastings in 1066. Those staying at One Aldwych, where rooms cost more than £1,000 a night, are able to get tickets to the tapestry exhibition through a corporate partnership with the British Museum.

As well as a viewing of the tapestry, guests who book the Bayeux experience also get a themed cocktail and a full English breakfast. The hotel says on its website: “Just a short stroll through Covent Garden and Bloomsbury brings you to the British Museum, our official partner for this landmark season. Here, one of the most anticipated cultural events of our lifetime unfolds: the Bayeux tapestry on view, a loan from France in a historic, once-in-a-generation agreement.” Dollimore said: “It is outrageous that one of London’s most expensive hotels has been offered this access to the Bayeux tapestry. How can it be right that some are able to pay their way in while others have to scramble for a chance to see this piece of our heritage?”

But the show is also proving controversial, and not only because when advance tickets went on sale for museum members earlier this month they complained of hour-long queues at the online checkout. Although the tapestry has already been removed from display in Normandy – concertinaed into a special crate and placed in storage while the Bayeux Tapestry Museum undergoes extensive redevelopment before reopening next year – there are concerns that it could suffer damage while travelling farther afield to London via Kent, where it was probably designed and embroidered in the years immediately following the Conquest of 1066.

British Museum’s £33 tickets sold out in a day but some slots have been reserved for guests at five-star One Aldwych

Those hoping to snare a glimpse of the Bayeux tapestry when it comes to the British Museum this September faced nine-hour online queues, with the £33 tickets sold out within a day.

But the monied guests of a five-star hotel in Covent Garden have not had to go to such arduous lengths to get a view of the nearly 1,000-year-old depiction of William the Conqueror’s victory over King Harold II of England at Hastings in 1066.

Those staying at One Aldwych, where rooms cost more than £1,000 a night, are able to get tickets to the tapestry exhibition through a corporate partnership with the British Museum.

Helena Dollimore, the MP for Hastings and Rye, said it was “outrageous” that those who could afford to pay for an expensive hotel room got free access to the exhibition while others had to scramble for tickets.

Dollimore has been negotiating with the museum to get access for children of “1066 country”, which she represents, to see the exhibition free of charge.

Hotel guests are told they can select any date and time during their stay to be prioritised for tickets, and that there are “plenty of tickets”. However, there is a limit of one ticket per guest per stay.

As well as a viewing of the tapestry, guests who book the Bayeux experience also get a themed cocktail and a full English breakfast. The hotel says on its website: “Just a short stroll through Covent Garden and Bloomsbury brings you to the British Museum, our official partner for this landmark season. Here, one of the most anticipated cultural events of our lifetime unfolds: the Bayeux tapestry on view, a loan from France in a historic, once-in-a-generation agreement.”

Dollimore said: “It is outrageous that one of London’s most expensive hotels has been offered this access to the Bayeux tapestry. How can it be right that some are able to pay their way in while others have to scramble for a chance to see this piece of our heritage?”

There has been huge interest in seeing the tapestry in the museum as it has arrived on English shores for the first time since it was made. The first batch of tickets, which are sold out, were for slots between September and December. Two releases will follow in October and January for the remainder of the tapestry’s stay in Britain, which runs until July 2027.

"A lovely idea, but it's never going to happen."

For years, that was how colleagues at Normandy's Bayeux Tapestry Museum responded whenever English medievalist Michael Lewis suggested that the 11th-century embroidery should return to Britain for the first time in a millennium. Yet, thanks in large part to his persistence, those doubters are about to be proved wrong.

This autumn, the Bayeux Tapestry – which depicts the death of the last Anglo-Saxon king, Harold II, at the Battle of Hastings – will appear in a landmark British Museum exhibition, curated by Lewis. Across a 10-month run, the museum expects a million visitors, which would make it one of its most popular exhibitions ever, joining the ranks of The First Emperor: China's Terracotta Army, which had 800,000 visitors in 2007-8; and The Treasures of Tutankhamun blockbuster of 1972, which attracted almost 1,700,000.

If, like me, you've only encountered images of the tapestry online or in books – where its continuous frieze is broken up into piecemeal scenes – the show should, in addition to providing a history lesson about the Norman Conquest, reveal the monumentality of an artefact that, at 224ft, is as long as a football pitch is wide. For Nicholas Cullinan, the British Museum's director, it's more than an exhibition: "It's a national cultural moment, a piece of international diplomacy," he tells me, "and a hugely historic moment."

But the show is also proving controversial, and not only because when advance tickets went on sale for museum members earlier this month they complained of hour-long queues at the online checkout. Although the tapestry has already been removed from display in Normandy – concertinaed into a special crate and placed in storage while the Bayeux Tapestry Museum undergoes extensive redevelopment before reopening next year – there are concerns that it could suffer damage while travelling farther afield to London via Kent, where it was probably designed and embroidered in the years immediately following the Conquest of 1066.

According to the French art historian and commentator Didier Rykner, who last summer organised a petition, signed by tens of thousands of people, to stop the loan (and whom I met in Paris earlier this year), "everybody who knows" about historical textiles believes that moving the tapestry is "a menace". Tickets to see the Bayeux Tapestry sold out in just over 24 hours as thousands of people scrambled to secure their place.

The British Museum said it had enjoyed its biggest ever day of ticket sales thanks to unprecedented demand to see the 11th-century embroidery.

After tickets went on sale at 10am on Wednesday, the online queue reached a peak of more than 80,000 people waiting to buy tickets.

The museum had warned of Glastonbury-style waiting times and appeared to experience some trouble coping with demand on its website.

Users reported being told the queue was paused while a message encouraged people to “be patient”.

On Thursday morning, more than 40,000 new hopefuls were in the queue. The British Museum then announced that all tickets in this batch had sold out.

A spokesman said: “The museum generated over £2.5m through sales, bigger in one day than any other exhibition ever held.
